terms.name: AI / machine learning / deep learning
terms.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of building systems for tasks such as recognizing objects or understanding speech. Machine learning is one approach to AI: a system learns a rule from examples. Deep learning is a type of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers.
terms.example: Sorting messages by learned patterns is machine learning. A modern language model is a deep-learning system.
terms.trap: These labels describe overlapping levels of a field, not three competing products.

terms.name: Model vs application
terms.definition: A trained model takes an input and computes an output using numbers it learned during training. An application decides what to send the model, which tools it can use, and what the user sees.
terms.example: A chat app may search the web using a separate tool, then ask a model to write the answer.
terms.trap: A product feature is not necessarily a capability inside the model weights.

terms.name: LLM — large language model
terms.definition: A large language model learns patterns in sequences of text fragments called tokens. To generate a reply, a model such as GPT predicts one token, adds it to the text, then predicts the next.
terms.example: The same model can draft a letter, explain a paragraph or translate a sentence.
terms.trap: Fluent output is not a guarantee of correct facts or sound reasoning.

terms.name: Token
terms.definition: A token is one unit in the sequence a model receives or generates. In text, a token might be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or even a single byte.
terms.example: A long technical word may use several tokens even though you count it as one word.
terms.trap: There is no universal tokens-per-word ratio across languages and tokenizers.

terms.name: Tokenizer
terms.definition: A text tokenizer splits text into tokens and maps each one to a number in a fixed vocabulary. Those numbers tell the model which tokens appeared and in what order.
terms.example: Two models can split the same supplier specification differently.
terms.trap: Token counts can differ even when the visible text is identical.

terms.name: Parameters / weights
terms.definition: Parameters are numbers the model adjusts during training. A weight is one kind of parameter: it controls how much an input contributes to another calculation.
terms.example: An 8B model has roughly eight billion parameters.
terms.trap: More parameters do not automatically mean a better result on your task.

terms.name: Embedding
terms.definition: An embedding represents an item, such as a word or a passage, as a list of numbers. A search model can learn to give a question and a useful passage similar vectors, even when they use different words.
terms.example: A document search system compares a question’s representation with representations of stored passages.
terms.trap: Similar representations do not prove that two statements are equally true.

terms.name: Attention
terms.definition: Attention lets one position in a sequence incorporate information from other positions. It assigns each available position a weight and adds up the information from those positions in those proportions.
terms.example: To interpret “it,” useful context may include a noun mentioned earlier in the sentence.
terms.trap: Attention weights are not a complete explanation of a model’s decision.

terms.name: Transformer
terms.definition: A Transformer is a neural network that updates the representation of each token using information from other tokens. Its self-attention layers determine how much information to take from each available position.
terms.example: Many later language models adapt this architecture for understanding or generating text.
terms.trap: A shared architecture name does not mean all models use the same training data or design.

terms.name: Multimodal
terms.definition: A multimodal model works with more than one kind of input or output, such as images and text. A model that answers a written question about a photograph uses both kinds of input.
terms.example: A model reads a chart image and answers a written question about it.
terms.trap: Supported input types and tool access differ between particular models and products.

terms.name: Pre-training
terms.definition: During pretraining, a model learns from a broad collection of examples. A common task for a language model is to predict missing or upcoming tokens. The resulting weights can be adapted for other tasks.
terms.example: A model develops general language capabilities before being adapted for a narrower role.
terms.trap: Pre-training is not the same as opening your document during a conversation.

terms.name: Fine-tuning
terms.definition: Fine-tuning starts with a trained model and gives it additional training on selected examples. The training changes some of its existing weights or a smaller set of added weights.
terms.example: Train on examples of well-written inspection reports to improve a consistent report style.
terms.trap: It is not a reliable substitute for retrieving a changing inventory database.

terms.name: Post-training
terms.definition: Post-training is the training a model receives after pretraining. For example, a team might use sample instructions with good answers to teach a model how to follow requests.
terms.example: A model learns to answer requests in a more useful format.
terms.trap: The label covers different methods; it does not identify a single recipe.

terms.name: Inference
terms.definition: Inference means running a trained model on an input to obtain a prediction or response. When you ask a chat model a new question, it usually answers with its weights fixed.
terms.example: You submit a question and receive a generated answer.
terms.trap: Ordinary inference does not necessarily change the model’s weights.

terms.name: Loss
terms.definition: A loss function assigns a number to a prediction according to a chosen rule. Training tries to reduce the average loss across examples. For instance, a prediction of 12 for a target of 10 has a squared error of 4.
terms.example: Training adjusts weights to reduce prediction error on examples.
terms.trap: Lower training loss does not guarantee better real-world usefulness.

terms.name: RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback
terms.definition: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, people's judgments guide a model's training. In one common method, people rank answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the language model learns to produce answers with higher predicted rewards.
terms.example: People prefer one answer to another, helping shape a training signal.
terms.trap: Preferred answers are not always factually correct.

terms.name: Distillation
terms.definition: In distillation, one model supplies training examples or target probabilities for another model. The model being trained learns to reproduce aspects of the first model's behavior.
terms.example: A smaller model learns from examples produced by a stronger model.
terms.trap: The student need not preserve all of the teacher’s abilities or limitations in the same way.

terms.name: LoRA / adapters
terms.definition: LoRA adapts a model by keeping an original weight matrix fixed and learning a change to it. It represents the change as the product of two smaller matrices, which reduces how many numbers training must adjust.
terms.example: Customize a general model without updating every original parameter.
terms.trap: Training fewer parameters does not eliminate the need to run or store the base model.

terms.name: Prompt
terms.definition: A prompt is the input that sets the task for a model. It can include the question, instructions, examples, and documents the model should use.
terms.example: Ask for a comparison table and provide the quotations to compare.
terms.trap: Better wording cannot supply missing evidence by itself.

terms.name: Context window
terms.definition: A context window limits how many tokens a model can use in one request. In models with a shared limit, instructions, conversation history, supplied documents, and the new reply all use part of that allowance.
terms.example: A request includes instructions, conversation history and excerpts from a paper.
terms.trap: A large advertised limit does not guarantee perfect retrieval of every detail.

terms.name: RAG — retrieval-augmented generation
terms.definition: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), software searches an external collection for relevant passages and includes them in the model's input. The model then writes an answer using that material.
terms.example: Find passages in an equipment manual before answering a maintenance question.
terms.trap: Bad retrieval or unsupported generation can still produce a wrong answer.

terms.name: Hallucination
terms.definition: A hallucination is a generated detail that conflicts with the evidence or lacks support where evidence is required. For example, a model might invent a delivery date when the order only says “pending.”
terms.example: A plausible-looking research citation turns out not to exist.
terms.trap: Confidence, detail and good formatting do not establish truth.

terms.name: Reasoning tokens / test-time compute
terms.definition: Test-time compute is the computation a system uses while answering. Some models spend part of it on intermediate tokens before the final answer. A system can also try several answers and check which ones work.
terms.example: A difficult problem receives more work before the final answer is returned.
terms.trap: More computation can cost more and still lead to an incorrect answer.

terms.name: Temperature
terms.definition: Temperature controls how strongly sampling favors tokens with higher scores. Lowering it concentrates probability on the highest-scoring choices. Raising it spreads probability more evenly across choices.
terms.example: Lower settings often produce more repeatable wording; higher settings can increase variation.
terms.trap: It is not a truthfulness control, and not every model exposes it.

terms.name: Agent
terms.definition: An agent uses a model to choose actions as a task unfolds. After a tool returns a result, the model can use that result to decide what to do next.
terms.example: Read files, run a calculation, inspect the result and revise a report.
terms.trap: The term is used loosely; ask which actions and checks the system actually performs.

terms.name: Workflow vs agent
terms.definition: In a predefined workflow, software specifies the order of operations and the conditions for each branch. In an agent, a model chooses at least some of the next steps based on what has happened so far.
terms.example: A fixed invoice extraction pipeline differs from an assistant investigating why numbers disagree.
terms.trap: An agent is not automatically the best choice for a predictable, simple task.

terms.name: Tool / API
terms.definition: A tool lets an application carry out an operation, such as searching records or calculating a total. An API is the interface that tells other software how to request the operation and read its result.
terms.example: A spreadsheet tool calculates totals; a search tool retrieves pages.
terms.trap: Writing “I sent the email” is different from a successful email tool action.

terms.name: Harness / orchestration
terms.definition: A harness is the software around a model that manages a task. It prepares inputs, runs tool requests, passes results back to the model, and decides when execution should stop.
terms.example: The same model can perform differently with different search tools and retry rules.
terms.trap: A benchmark result may reflect the whole setup, not just the underlying model.

terms.name: Verification
terms.definition: Verification checks whether a specific result satisfies a requirement. For example, open the saved spreadsheet and compare its total with an independent calculation from the source rows.
terms.example: Reconcile the extracted quotation total with the original document and a calculation.
terms.trap: A second generated opinion is not independent verification by itself.

terms.name: GPU / accelerator
terms.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) can perform many numerical operations in parallel. GPUs and other accelerators are useful for the large matrix calculations in neural networks.
terms.example: A server uses accelerators for model computation while other software manages files and requests.
terms.trap: Chip count alone does not describe usable performance; memory, networking and software also matter.

terms.name: VRAM / HBM / model memory
terms.definition: A GPU stores data in device memory, often called VRAM. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is one technology used for that memory. A running model needs space for its weights, cached values, and temporary calculations.
terms.example: A model may need space for stored parameters, conversation caches and temporary calculations.
terms.trap: A weights-only size estimate is not a full hardware requirement.

terms.name: Quantization
terms.definition: Quantization maps a range of numbers to a smaller set of possible values. Storing each weight with fewer bits can save memory. The rounding involved can change the model's output.
terms.example: A lower-bit representation can reduce the memory occupied by model weights.
terms.trap: Quality and speed depend on the method and hardware; fewer bits are not a universal speed guarantee.

terms.name: MoE — mixture of experts
terms.definition: A mixture-of-experts layer contains several smaller networks called experts. In a sparse version, a router chooses a few experts for each token and combines their outputs.
terms.example: A router sends a token through a small subset of available experts.
terms.trap: Experts are learned subnetworks, not necessarily human-readable subject departments.

terms.name: Total vs active parameters
terms.definition: The total parameter count includes all the model's weights. In a sparse model, only some take part in processing a given token. Those weights, including weights in shared layers, are its active parameters for that token.
terms.example: A sparse model may store many experts but use only a subset for a token.
terms.trap: The active count is not the amount of memory needed to store the whole model.

terms.name: KV cache
terms.definition: During text generation, a Transformer can save two vectors from each earlier token at each attention layer: its key and its value. Reusing them lets the next token attend to earlier tokens without computing those vectors again.
terms.example: While generating a reply, a model can reuse keys and values it already computed for earlier tokens.
terms.trap: This working state is not the same thing as permanent personal memory.

terms.name: Prefill vs decode
terms.definition: During prefill, a model processes the prompt and computes the scores for the first output token. During decoding, it uses the tokens generated so far to predict the following tokens, one step at a time.
terms.example: You first wait for an answer to start, then watch it stream.
terms.trap: Long input and long output stress a serving system differently.

terms.name: Latency / TTFT
terms.definition: Latency is elapsed time. Time to first token (TTFT) runs from sending the request to receiving its first output token. Total latency runs until the response is complete.
terms.example: A reply can start quickly yet take a long time to finish.
terms.trap: One waiting-time metric does not describe the entire experience.

terms.name: Throughput / batching
terms.definition: Throughput measures how much work a system completes in a given time, such as output tokens per second across all users. Batching lets the hardware process parts of several requests together.
terms.example: A server handles many users concurrently rather than dedicating a whole accelerator to each one.
terms.trap: Higher total throughput does not necessarily mean a shorter wait for each user.

terms.name: Benchmark
terms.definition: A benchmark specifies tasks and rules for scoring them. To interpret a score, check what the system was asked to do and what data, tools, and resources it could use.
terms.example: A coding benchmark checks solutions under a particular set of tools, budgets and tests.
terms.trap: One leaderboard score is not a universal measure of intelligence or business value.

terms.name: Ablation
terms.definition: An ablation study removes or changes one part of a system, then repeats the evaluation. The difference in results estimates that part's contribution in the tested setup.
terms.example: Compare the same training setup with and without a new attention mechanism.
terms.trap: Several simultaneous changes make it harder to identify which change caused a gain.

terms.name: Checkpoint / model weights
terms.definition: A checkpoint saves the state of a model at a particular point in training. Its weights can be loaded for prediction. Resuming training exactly may also require the optimizer state and the position in the training data.
terms.example: A research team releases a downloadable version of its trained model.
terms.trap: A checkpoint alone may not include training data, full training code or deployment software.

terms.name: Open weights / open source
terms.definition: An open-weight release makes trained weights available under stated terms. To decide whether you can run, modify, or redistribute the model, examine the license and the code, data, and documentation supplied with it.
terms.example: A downloadable model may still have a custom license or restricted uses.
terms.trap: Availability, permission to use commercially, and reproducibility are separate questions.

terms.name: Preprint / technical report / announcement
terms.definition: A preprint makes a research manuscript publicly available, often before peer review. A technical report describes work in detail. A release announcement tells readers what was released. A single publication can serve more than one role.
terms.example: A release blog can establish an announcement date without providing a complete reproducible experiment.
terms.trap: Public availability does not by itself establish peer review or independent replication.

terms.name: FLOPs / compute budget
terms.definition: FLOPs count floating-point arithmetic operations such as additions and multiplications. A training compute budget can specify how many of these operations are available. FLOPs per second measures the rate at which they run.
terms.example: Two training runs may allocate a fixed budget differently between model size and training data.
terms.trap: An operation count is not a direct measurement of wall-clock time or money.

terms.name: Gradient
terms.definition: The gradient of a loss is the vector of its partial derivatives. Each component tells you how the loss changes locally if you vary one parameter while holding the others fixed.
terms.example: For L=(x²+3y²)/2, the gradient is (x,3y). At (1,1), a small change in y has three times the first-order effect of the same change in x.
terms.trap: The gradient uses local information. Curvature determines how far a linear prediction stays accurate.

terms.name: Gradient descent
terms.definition: Gradient descent subtracts a multiple of the current gradient from the parameters, then recomputes the gradient at the new point. A sufficiently small step lowers a smooth loss when the gradient is nonzero.
terms.example: At (1,1), subtracting 0.1(1,3) gives (0.9,0.7). Inspect the orange path in the loss-surface model.
terms.trap: Large steps can overshoot a minimum even with the correct gradient.

terms.name: Learning rate
terms.definition: In gradient descent, the learning rate multiplies the gradient to set the size of each parameter update. Doubling the rate doubles the first step from the same starting point.
terms.example: With gradient 4, a learning rate of 0.05 makes a step of magnitude 0.2.
terms.trap: A single learning rate produces different step lengths as gradient magnitudes change.

terms.name: Curvature and Hessian
terms.definition: The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives of a smooth loss. Its eigenvalues give the local curvature along its eigenvectors. Greater curvature means the slope changes faster in that direction.
terms.example: For (x²+3y²)/2 the Hessian is diagonal with entries 1 and 3. The bowl is steeper along y.
terms.trap: For a positive-definite quadratic, constant-step gradient descent converges for 0 < η < 2/λmax. A general neural loss can have different local geometry.

terms.name: Stochastic gradient descent
terms.definition: Stochastic gradient descent uses a sample of the training data to estimate the gradient for each update. Different samples can give different update directions at the same weights.
terms.example: Use 32 examples to estimate the direction for one training step.
terms.trap: The sampled direction can differ from the full-data gradient at the same weights.

terms.name: Mini-batch
terms.definition: A mini-batch is a group of examples processed together during training. A common update uses the average gradient over the examples in that group.
terms.example: A batch of eight equally weighted losses contributes their mean to a simple objective.
terms.trap: Gradient accumulation can combine several small batches before one update.

terms.name: Epoch
terms.definition: An epoch is one complete pass through a training dataset. With 1,000 examples and batches of 50, one epoch contains 20 batches.
terms.example: With 1,000 examples and batches of 50, one full pass has 20 batches.
terms.trap: For a data stream, reporting training tokens or steps can be clearer than reporting epochs.

terms.name: Backpropagation
terms.definition: Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute how the loss changes with each weight. It works backward from the loss through the operations that produced it.
terms.example: If u=wx and L=u²/2, then ∂L/∂w=u·x.
terms.trap: The optimizer uses these derivatives to choose an update.

terms.name: Regularization
terms.definition: Regularization changes how a model is trained to help it perform well on new examples. One method adds a penalty for large weights to the loss, so fitting the data and keeping weights small both affect the result.
terms.example: Adding λ‖w‖² to the data loss penalizes large weights.
terms.trap: Excessive regularization can also hurt performance on unseen data.

terms.name: Vector
terms.definition: A vector is an ordered list of numbers in a specified coordinate system. When a vector represents measurements, each position must keep its meaning and unit across examples.
terms.example: The toy point (2,1,0) has three coordinates. A learned embedding may have hundreds or thousands.
terms.trap: Feature scales affect distance comparisons between points.

terms.name: Euclidean norm
terms.definition: The Euclidean norm is the length of a vector. Square each component, add the squares, then take the square root.
terms.example: The vector (3,4) has length 5. Dividing it by 5 gives a unit vector.
terms.trap: Normalizing a zero vector requires special handling.

terms.name: Dot product
terms.definition: The dot product adds the products of matching components of two vectors. It depends on both their lengths and the angle between them.
terms.example: (1,2)·(3,4)=11. Multiplying one vector by two doubles the dot product.
terms.trap: High vector norms can dominate scores even when directions differ.

terms.name: Cosine similarity
terms.definition: Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between two nonzero vectors. Compute it by dividing their dot product by the product of their lengths. It equals 1 for the same direction and 0 for perpendicular directions.
terms.example: (1,0) and (5,0) have cosine similarity 1. Turn one through 90° and the score becomes 0.
terms.trap: Similarity depends on the representation learned for the task.

terms.name: Euclidean distance
terms.definition: Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance between two points. Subtract their coordinate vectors, then take the Euclidean norm of that difference.
terms.example: Between (1,2) and (4,6), the difference is (3,4) and the distance is 5.
terms.trap: On unit vectors, squared distance equals 2−2 cos θ. With varying lengths, rankings can change.

terms.name: Softmax
terms.definition: Softmax converts scores into positive weights that add up to one. Exponentiate each score, then divide each result by the sum of all the exponentials. A larger score gets a larger weight.
terms.example: Three equal scores each receive weight 1/3. Adding the same constant to all scores preserves every weight.
terms.trap: A normalized score can still be a poor estimate of real-world probability.

terms.name: Causal mask
terms.definition: A causal mask controls which token positions can contribute to each prediction. In a standard decoder, a position can use its own token and earlier tokens to predict the next one.
terms.example: At token four, block scores for positions five and later before normalizing attention weights.
terms.trap: The mask enforces an information boundary even when training positions are processed together.

terms.name: Positional encoding
terms.definition: Positional encoding supplies information about the order of tokens. The original Transformer adds a pattern of sine and cosine values to each token's vector, using a different pattern for each position.
terms.example: The original Transformer adds sinusoidal signals at multiple frequencies to token embeddings.
terms.trap: Later architectures encode position in other ways, so check the paper’s actual mechanism.

terms.name: Train, validation and test splits
terms.definition: The training set is used to fit model weights. The validation set helps choose settings or compare designs. A separate test set estimates how the chosen system performs on new examples.
terms.example: Tune a retrieval threshold on validation queries, then evaluate once on held-out test queries.
terms.trap: Repeatedly tuning against the test set compromises its independence.

terms.name: Overfitting
terms.definition: A model overfits when it learns details specific to the training examples that hurt its performance on new examples. One warning sign is falling training error alongside rising validation error.
terms.example: Training error keeps falling while validation error begins to climb.
terms.trap: Check distribution shifts and label quality when interpreting a train–validation gap.

terms.name: Precision
terms.definition: Precision asks how many of the items a system marked positive really were positive. For a search engine, that means the fraction of returned pages that are relevant.
terms.example: If 8 of 10 retrieved pages are relevant, retrieval precision is 8/10.
terms.trap: Precision alone omits relevant items the system missed.

terms.name: Recall
terms.definition: Recall asks how many of all the positive items a system found. For a search engine, that means the fraction of all relevant pages in the collection that appeared in the results.
terms.example: If the collection contains 20 relevant pages and retrieval returns 8, recall is 8/20.
terms.trap: Computing recall requires knowing or estimating how many relevant items exist.

terms.name: Baseline
terms.definition: A baseline is a reference method against which you evaluate a new method. Testing both on the same cases makes the difference in their scores easier to interpret.
terms.example: Compare a retrieval assistant with the same generator receiving no retrieved passages.
terms.trap: Match evaluation tasks, budgets and scoring rules for a meaningful comparison.

terms.name: Data leakage
terms.definition: Data leakage occurs when information that should be unavailable influences training or evaluation. Examples include giving a forecast the actual outcome or including a copy of a test question in the training data.
terms.example: A classifier predicting late deliveries accidentally sees the final arrival date.
terms.trap: Leakage can inflate measured performance even when the model code is correct.

terms.name: Calibration
terms.definition: A model is well calibrated if events it assigns a given probability occur about that often. For instance, among many comparable predictions assigned 80% confidence, about 80% should be correct.
terms.example: Among many predictions assigned about 80% confidence, roughly 80% should be correct for good calibration in that range.
terms.trap: Calibration can change when the deployment population changes.

terms.name: State-space model
terms.definition: A state-space model updates an internal state as inputs arrive and uses that state to compute the output. Which earlier inputs still influence the output depends on the update rule.
terms.example: For dh/dt = −ah + 1, a > 0 and h(0)=0, the response approaches 1/a with time constant 1/a.
terms.trap: This scalar illustration has fixed coefficients. Selective sequence models can change their dynamics with the input.

facts.title: Who builds each part of an AI product?
facts.fact: One company may design the chips, another may train the model, and a third may build the application. Some companies do more than one of these jobs.
facts.example: A faster chip might return an answer sooner. Better document search might help the application answer a question it previously got wrong.
facts.ask: What changed for the person using the product?

facts.title: What does the application add to the model?
facts.fact: An application can retrieve documents, call other software, and check actions. Its design determines what the user can actually do.
facts.example: A model can suggest a spreadsheet formula. To put it in cell B2, the application also needs access to the sheet and a way to edit that cell.
facts.ask: Are we evaluating the model alone or the full system?

facts.title: What can a parameter count tell you?
facts.fact: A parameter count tells you how many adjustable numbers a model has. For a sparse model, check how many of those numbers are used to process one token.
facts.example: Two models with similar counts can produce very different results when asked to copy quantities from invoices.
facts.ask: Were both models tested on the same task with the same tools?

facts.title: What else uses memory while a model runs?
facts.fact: When a model writes a reply, it needs memory for its weights, for information it keeps from earlier tokens, and for temporary calculations.
facts.example: Eight billion weights at two bytes per weight occupy 16 GB before the system processes a single request.
facts.ask: Does the memory estimate include answering several users at once?

facts.title: How much does one completed task cost?
facts.fact: A system may pay to process the question, generate the answer, use tools and try again. Count each of those costs when comparing models.
facts.example: Model A spends $12 and answers 80 questions correctly. Model B spends $10 and gets 50 right. Each correct answer costs 15 cents with A and 20 cents with B.
facts.ask: What is the cost per accepted result, including checks and retries?

facts.title: Which measure of speed matters here?
facts.fact: A reader can measure the wait for the first word and the wait for the full answer. A server operator may instead measure how much text the system produces for all users in a second.
facts.example: One reply can start sooner but finish later than another. Record both times if you care about reading the full answer.
facts.ask: How long were the questions and answers, and how many users were sharing the server?

facts.title: Read the evaluation setup before comparing scores
facts.fact: Task versions, tools, prompts, effort, budgets and scoring rules affect measured results.
facts.example: A model allowed to run its code can check for errors that a model limited to one written answer must catch on its own.
facts.ask: Did both systems get the same tasks, tools, and budget?

facts.title: How much text fits, and how well can the model use it?
facts.fact: The context window limits how many tokens a request can contain. For some models, the input and answer share that space. Check the model card for the exact limits.
facts.example: A model can accept a long manual yet overlook an exception buried near the end.
facts.ask: Was performance tested on the kind of long-document question you need?

facts.title: Retrieval and fine-tuning have different jobs
facts.fact: With retrieval, software finds a passage and gives it to the model for this answer. With fine-tuning, additional training changes some of the numbers the model uses to produce later answers.
facts.example: Look up today’s stock count in the inventory table. If the goal is to produce reports in a consistent style, examples of well-written reports can help.
facts.ask: Do you need fresh evidence, a changed behavior, or both?

facts.title: What are you allowed to do with a downloaded model?
facts.fact: A release may include the trained weights, the training code, or both. Its license sets the conditions for using and distributing those materials.
facts.example: A release may include weights while leaving important training details unavailable.
facts.ask: What exactly is provided, and under what terms?

facts.title: What can a result tell you about the model behind it?
facts.fact: A score shows how the tested system performed. Determining how many parameters it has, what it trained on or how it was trained requires other evidence.
facts.example: A coding improvement could reflect training, tools or serving changes.
facts.ask: Which technical details were actually disclosed?

facts.title: What evidence does each publication provide?
facts.fact: A release note tells readers when a feature became available. An experiment can measure its effect under specified conditions. If another team repeats the experiment, readers can compare the two results.
facts.example: One successful demonstration shows the task is possible in that setting. To estimate success rate, you also need the number of attempts and how often they failed.
facts.ask: What is the claim, who measured it, and can the conditions be inspected?

facts.title: How can you tell whether an agent completed a task?
facts.fact: An agent can describe an action even when the tool it called failed. Check the system where the change was supposed to happen.
facts.example: If the task was to reserve five bags, open the inventory system and check the reservation quantity and order number.
facts.ask: What evidence shows the intended action completed correctly?

facts.title: What limits performance on this workload?
facts.fact: An operation can spend most of its time doing arithmetic, reading values from memory, or exchanging them between devices. A speedup helps most when it shortens the step that takes the most time.
facts.example: A change that saves attention memory may help long documents more than short replies.
facts.ask: Which resource limits this particular workload?

examples.title: Compare supplier quotations
examples.goal: Compare the delivered price for the same quantity in three PDF quotations.
flow: Find the three quotations and check their dates.
Extract product, quantity, currency, unit and delivery terms.
Put prices in the same unit and currency. Include freight only when the quotation states it or provides enough information to calculate it.
Check each important value against its source page.
examples.lesson: A calculator can multiply the right numbers and still answer the wrong question. If one quotation is per bag and another is per tonne, first establish how much a bag weighs.

examples.title: Ask about an equipment manual
examples.goal: Find the procedure that applies to a specific model and condition.
flow: Identify the manual version and equipment.
Retrieve the relevant instructions and exceptions.
Answer with source pages and state missing information.
Have a responsible person check the applicable procedure.
examples.lesson: A general instruction and its exception can be on different pages. Cite both so the reader can check which one applies to this machine.

examples.title: Understand a new research paper
examples.goal: Explain the main contribution without reading every equation first.
flow: Read the problem and main result.
Look up unfamiliar terms.
Identify the comparison method in the results table. Find the row that adds or changes the method being studied.
Check the experiment and limitations before generalizing.
examples.lesson: If the authors change both the training data and the model, the difference in scores alone cannot tell you which change helped.

examples.title: Build a weekly operations report
examples.goal: Turn logs and tables into a concise, traceable update.
flow: Collect the relevant logs and tables for the same week.
Separate recorded facts from plans and missing data.
Use the same units and date range for all totals.
Draft the report and reconcile its figures with the inputs.
examples.lesson: If the weekly report always uses the same tables, software can calculate the totals in fixed steps. The model can then draft the explanation from those totals.

examples.title: Create a consistent technical writing style
examples.goal: Produce reports with stable terminology and structure.
flow: Start with a clear template and examples in the prompt.
Keep frequently changing facts in external records.
Try the template on several reports, including one with missing data.
Consider fine-tuning only if simpler methods do not meet the need.
examples.lesson: A sample report can teach the model your preferred headings. For this week’s figures, give it this week’s records.

quiz.question: You need answers from a frequently changing inventory table. What should supply the current figures?
options: Retrieve or query the current table.
Assume fine-tuning permanently keeps the figures current.
Choose the model with the largest parameter count.
quiz.explanation: Current evidence should come from the current records. Fine-tuning changes a model, but does not automatically synchronize a database.

quiz.question: A sparse model reports 100B total parameters and 10B active per token. Which statement follows?
options: Only 10B parameters need to be stored in every deployment.
Some computation uses a subset; the total storage requirement is a separate question.
It must be ten times faster than a 100B dense model.
quiz.explanation: Active computation and stored capacity are different. Hardware, communication and other work also affect speed.

quiz.question: An app says “I updated the file.” What is the strongest check?
options: Another model agrees that an update sounds plausible.
Inspect the saved file and validate the requested changes.
quiz.explanation: Completion needs evidence from the actual artifact or action, rather than only a statement about it.

quiz.question: Model A scores higher than B on a chart. What should you check first?
options: Whether tasks, versions, tools and budgets are comparable.
Whether the two weight files are the same size.
Whether the chart rounds both scores to the same number of decimal places.
quiz.explanation: Evaluation conditions affect the meaning of a score. Compare the setup as well as the number.

quiz.question: An 8B model at 16 bits has a raw-weights estimate of roughly 16 GB. What does that number leave out?
options: Nothing; it is a complete deployment requirement.
Caches, temporary state and other serving overhead.
quiz.explanation: The calculator estimates raw weight storage only. Actual serving memory also depends on workload and implementation.

quiz.question: A model accepts a very long document. What can you conclude?
options: Every detail will be recalled and applied correctly.
The model must have trained on that exact document.
The input fits the supported limit; task accuracy still needs checking.
quiz.explanation: Context capacity is useful, but the model can still miss details or make unsupported connections.
